1:
Chrysostom makes the verse a lesson in how authority should speak. It is the virtue of teachers, he says, to aim not at praise nor at esteem from those under them but at their salvation, since a man who made the other his aim would be not a teacher but a tyrant; God did not set him over them that he should enjoy greater court and service, but that his own interests should be disregarded and every one of theirs built up. Paul he takes as the model, free from all manner of vanity, content to be one of the many and indeed the least of them, calling himself their servant and here writing nothing dictatorial, nothing imperious, but all chastened and subdued. Then he presses the word beseech in dialogue: what art thou beseeching, and is it that thou mayest gain some end for thyself? No, in no wise; it is that I may save others — and yet men who beseech do so for what matters to themselves, and this, Paul answers, does matter to me.

Whether the phrase is prisoner of the Lord or in the Lord is a small construal. Gill reports both, notes that some attach in the Lord to the verb rather than the noun so that Paul beseeches them in the Lord's name, and prefers the sense that he is a prisoner for the Lord's sake. Henry and Wesley take it the same way. Why Paul mentions his chains at all is answered four ways that do not exclude each other. Henry says he was not ashamed of his bonds, knowing he suffered not as an evildoer, and that the mention recommends his letter with greater tenderness, since a doctrine he thought worth suffering for they should surely think worth serious regard. Calvin turns the same fact into an argument from authority: his imprisonment, which might have been supposed to render him despised, confirms his commission, being the seal of the embassy with which he was honoured — and adds the sentence the passage is remembered for, that the apostle's prison is more truly venerable than the triumphal chariot of kings. Wesley makes it a motive of comfort, that their obedience would relieve him under it; Gill turns it the other way, that some professors by their walk added affliction to his bonds. Henry alone notices what the prisoner does not ask for — not relief, nor their interest used to obtain his liberty, which is the first thing prisoners commonly solicit of their friends, but only that they would approve themselves good Christians.

What walking worthily amounts to is where Ellicott does his best work. Being worthy of the Christian calling might show itself in any grace of regenerate humanity, all being features of the image of Christ; elsewhere the same demand issues in holiness, elsewhere in steadfastness of faith. But here, he argues, the point dwelt on in their calling has been that they were aliens, helpless and miserable, and are now united in one body with the ancient people of God — so the graces named as answering to that calling are humility and gentleness, teaching them to sink all thought of self in the unity of the Spirit. The virtues are thus derived from the particular argument of the letter rather than from a general list.

Calvin sets out the structure first: the three remaining chapters consist entirely of practical exhortation, mutual agreement is the first subject, and church government is discussed within it because our Lord framed that government to maintain unity. Barnes and Clarke both open with an analysis of the whole chapter rather than a comment on the verse. Robertson keeps to the grammar, explaining the relative as attracted into the genitive of its antecedent, and notes that the list of virtues stands also in Colossians, where Paul singles out love as he adds it here.
2:
Calvin insists the four graces are given in a deliberate order, and that the order is the argument. Paul was about to enter on the subject of unity, to which humility is the first step; humility produces meekness, meekness disposes us to bear with our brethren, and forbearance preserves a unity that would otherwise be broken a hundred times a day. He then asks whence rudeness, pride and disdainful language toward brethren, whence quarrels, insults and reproaches — and answers that they come from every man carrying his self-love and regard to his own interests to excess. Hence the warning against taking the exhortations out of sequence: it is to no purpose to inculcate forbearance until the natural fierceness has been subdued and mildness acquired, and equally vain to discourse of meekness before beginning with humility.

The four terms are then defined, closely but not identically. Henry opposes each to its vice: lowliness is mean thoughts of ourselves, against pride; meekness makes men unwilling to provoke and not easily provoked, against angry resentment and peevishness; long-suffering is patient bearing of injuries without revenge; and forbearing in love means bearing infirmities so as not to cease loving on their account. Clarke renders the third literally as long-mindedness, never permitting a provocation to reach the end of your patience, and gives two senses of the fourth — sustaining one another through the miseries of life, or bearing with one another, knowing how much others have had to bear with us. Gill fills out lowliness practically: the meanest thoughts of oneself and the best of others, not envying the gifts of others but rejoicing at every increase of them, and willing to receive instruction from the meanest saints. Henry sums the whole under one head, that love is the law of Christ's kingdom, the lesson of his school, the livery of his family.

Whether the unity of the Spirit names the author of the unity or its kind is genuinely disputed. Barnes is flat that it does not refer to there being one Holy Spirit but to unity of affection, of confidence, of love, Christians united in temper and not split into factions. Calvin reports the other reading and declines it: some take it of the spiritual unity produced in us by the Spirit of God, who alone makes us of one accord and of one mind, but he thinks it more natural to understand the words as denoting harmony of views. Gill takes both at once, a union of the souls of men in spiritual affairs and effected by the Spirit by whom they are baptized into one body; Clarke likewise makes it not only spiritual but a unity of sentiments and affections springing from the Spirit; Wesley resolves it simply as a fruit of the Spirit. On the bond, Robertson notes that in the parallel epistle love is the bond rather than peace, and adds that there is no peace without love; Clarke describes a union in which the interests of all parties are concentrated, cemented and sealed, the Spirit being the seal upon the knot.

Both Clarke and Barnes explain why the exhortation was needed at Ephesus in particular. The church was composed of converted Jews and Gentiles brought up quite differently, and Clarke supposes the Jews might envy Gentiles admitted to the same privileges without bearing the yoke of the law; he notes too that the verb for endeavouring implies intense labour. Barnes gives the same local reason and generalises it: tastes and habits differ, intellect and feeling vary, education and temperament are unlike, so there is constant danger of division wherever men are brought together in one society. Gill draws three inferences from the mere fact that they are told to keep the unity — that it already exists, that it is valuable enough to be worth pains, and that it is difficult to secure.
4:
Ellicott hears the shape of the passage before its content. The Greek supplies no verb and starts with a striking abruption, with the terse concentration of thought and word that marks out an embryo creed — so that the seven unities are read as an early confession rather than a list. Wesley reaches the same compression from the other end, resolving Spirit, Lord and Father into the Trinity and the hope into heaven. Robertson takes two clauses as polemic: the one Spirit is grammatical neuter but not therefore an it, and the one Lord is Christ alone, with no intermediate beings.

What the one body is draws the widest answers. Chrysostom extends it through time — the faithful throughout the whole world, those who are and have been and shall be, with those who pleased God before Christ's coming counted in the same body. He also states the method he thinks Paul is using: when the apostle urges anything of special importance he grounds the exhortation on things in heaven. Gill multiplies the figures instead: one natural body, whose members should not bite and devour one another; one kingdom, which divided against itself cannot stand; one household, whose brethren should not fall out by the way. He guards the doctrine of God in passing, that the unity of the Godhead is not inconsistent with a trinity of persons in it. Barnes turns the doctrine against the divisions of his own day and is the most forceful voice here. The church is at present divided into many denominations, yet there is but one holy catholic church, and it should feel that it is one; Christ did not come to redeem different churches and give them different places in heaven, nor to save the Episcopalian or Presbyterian or Methodist communion only, nor merely the black man or the red or the white, nor to set up separate mansions in the skies for any of them.

Calvin presses the argument from the shared inheritance. The union must be of the whole man, not in part only but in body and soul, and since we are called to one inheritance and one life we cannot obtain eternal life without living in mutual harmony here; were it deeply impressed on us that we are under a law which no more permits the children of God to differ among themselves than it permits the kingdom of heaven to be divided, we should cultivate brotherly kindness in earnest.

Ellicott's note on the one faith and baptism is the most unexpected thing here, because he uses it to locate where Christendom divides. Nearly all Christians, even in the church's divided condition, are still united in the one baptism; and if the one faith is taken as the baptismal profession contains it, our divisions turn mainly on the subsidiary article concerning the Holy Catholic Church and not on the three primary articles of Father, Son and Holy Ghost. Robertson works the same clause lexically and guards it doctrinally: the noun names the result of baptizing rather than the act, and the one baptism is for all who confess Christ by this symbol — not that they are made disciples by it, but that they so profess him publicly. Clarke reads it as administered in the name of the Trinity and indicative of the influences and privileges of the Christian religion, and Calvin simply insists that what is one cannot be divided or rent.

On the one God, Barnes argues from monotheism to concord. Were there many gods there could be no more hope of unity than among the worshippers of Mammon and Bacchus, since men whose affections are set on different objects have no sympathy of feeling; but where there is one supreme object of attachment unity may be expected, as the children of a family devoted to one parent are united among themselves.
7:
What the grace given to every one is divides them. Clarke takes it of office: though equal in the respects just named, we have different situations to fill in church and world, and the free gift is according to the office and the office according to the gift. Barnes takes it of the gracious influences of the Spirit, and draws two rules from the phrase about measure: it is bestowed and not originated by ourselves, and it comes by a wise adaptation rather than without rule. Calvin turns the measure into an argument for dependence: no member can supply his own necessities without the rest, so each must throw his gift into the common stock, and none be proud of his attainments. Henry adds that the measure is never perfected here, since God's children are growing as long as they are in this world.

The quotation is the passage's great difficulty and nobody hides it. Barnes states it fully: the Psalm celebrates a moving of the ark, appears to have no relation to the Messiah, and would not occur to any reader as referring to the ascension had the apostle not so quoted it — so great difficulty has been felt about the principle on which Paul applied it. Calvin is blunter still, admitting at the outset that to serve his argument Paul has departed not a little from the true meaning of the quotation, and that wicked men charge him with unfair use of Scripture. His defence is not to deny the charge but to change the standard: Paul does not reason here as a logician about what necessarily follows from the prophet's words, and knew that David's language about God's ascension was metaphorical — yet it does bear reference to some previous humiliation on God's part, and that is what Paul infers. Wesley reaches a related point by a sharper route: the ascent implies a prior descent only on the supposition that the one ascending is God, since all the saints will ascend to heaven though none of them descended thence.

That Paul writes gave where the Psalm has received is noticed by all and explained by Ellicott. The change of person already shows a free quotation; but the verb for receiving is used constantly of fetching for another, and the Chaldee Targum glosses the place as thou hast given gifts to the sons of men — so Paul's rendering was already current, though the Targum applied it to Moses as mediator. On the imagery Clarke supplies a Roman triumph line by line: the conqueror in a high chariot, the conquered kings bound behind it, money thrown among the crowd, and the rebels who had fought against him sharing his munificence, since it is the property of a hero to be generous. No subject is expressed for he saith, and Robertson reports commentators dividing between God and the Scripture; Gill answers in three words, God in the Scripture. Cyril, expounding the Creed, treats the ascension as the article that follows the resurrection.

What the lower parts of the earth are is disputed. Barnes takes them for the lowest state of humiliation; Clarke reads the incarnation and the death; Robertson allows that if the ascent is the Ascension the descent is the Incarnation, and that what follows argues for this, but concedes the alternative of the descent into Hades. Ellicott states both and prefers the second: the reasoning would be satisfied by the earth as lower than heaven, but usage points to the regions beneath, which almost all ancient interpreters hold, and which suits the filling of all things and the leading captive of the powers of hell. Wesley cites a text for each sense without deciding. On the filling, Ellicott insists the words are too wide for any limitation, where Wesley confines them to the church filled with his Spirit and operations.
11:
That Paul writes gave where the parallel epistle has appointed is turned to account by Ellicott: the word is suggested by the quotation just made, and it follows that they who are ministers of his gifts are themselves gifts from him to the church.

Which of the offices were meant to last is agreed in substance. Gill calls the apostolate the first and chief office, extraordinary and now ceased. Barnes says all the offices existed then and all were proper, though not all were designed to be permanent; and on the evangelist he confesses the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and that what the office was can no longer be determined. Clarke agrees the offices and gifts are still necessary and still given, then complains that they do not know their places: in most churches there is but one office, that of preacher, apostles and prophets and evangelists and pastors and teachers all compounded into that single class, so that many to whom God has given nothing but a gift of exhortation take texts to explain them, and lose their time and mar their ministry.

Calvin asks why, in a discussion of the gifts of the Spirit, Paul should enumerate offices instead. His answer is that when men are called by God the two are inseparable, since God does not confer the mere name of apostle or pastor but endows with the gifts without which the office cannot be discharged;. At the next verse he anticipates the obvious objection — cannot the church be properly arranged without the instrumentality of men? — and answers that a ministry is required, this being the arrangement by which the Lord governs his church.

The word rendered perfecting is worked over by four. Robertson finds it late and rare, used by Galen medically and in the papyri of furnishing a house, and renders it the mending of the saints. Calvin traces it to the adjusting of parts possessing symmetry, as the members of a body are united in regular order, but prefers a word for ordering, in the sense in which a commonwealth is said to be ordered when confusion gives place to the regular administration of law. Ellicott disputes the shape of the whole verse: the three parallel clauses of the English do not correspond to the Greek, since the preposition of the first differs from that of the other two, signifying direction toward a thing where the others signify contact with it — so the first names the remoter object and the others the immediate consequence. He concedes that an early Greek expositor evidently saw nothing in the original to contradict the parallel rendering, and remarks that the construction would be greatly simplified if the first two clauses could be inverted. Wesley, by contrast, builds on the symmetry, finding the office of ministers here, the aim of the saints next, and the way of growing in grace in the three following, each with three parts in the same order.

On the unity of the faith Gill excludes two senses before settling: not the union between saints, nor that between Christ and his people, whose bond is his love and not their faith, but the one faith already named — either its doctrine, so that the ministry continues until watchmen and churches see eye to eye, or the grace of faith itself. Robertson gives the clause a polemical edge, setting the oneness of trust and full knowledge against the Gnostic vagaries disturbing it. On the perfect man Barnes disclaims sinless perfection and means only maturity as against childhood, while Clarke takes the measure at full height and turns it on his readers: many are studious to find how much inward sinfulness is consistent with a safe state in religion, but very few bring out the fair Gospel standard to try the stature of the church's members.
14:
In what sense Christians must stop being children is carefully bounded. Ellicott notes the word is almost always used in a bad sense, like our childish — not of the guilelessness or humility our Lord blessed, but of unforeseeing impulsiveness, and here of liability to change by every impression from without, so as to be everything by turns and nothing long. Gill keeps a place for the good sense: they should remain children in ardent love, in desire for the sincere milk, and in freedom from pride, malice and guile, but not in understanding. Calvin inserts a third stage between the two the verse names. Children are those who have not advanced a step in the way of the Lord and still hesitate, always wavering; those well founded in the doctrine of Christ, though not yet perfect, have wisdom enough to choose properly and go steadily — so the believer's life resembles youth, and at no period of this life are we men.

Wesley reads the two participles as two distinct dangers, and the distinction is the best small observation here: the fluctuation is from within, even when there is no wind, and the being carried about is from without, when we are assaulted by others themselves unstable as the wind. Barnes keeps to the sea — a vessel with no firmness, no settled course, no helm —. On the sleight of men all agree the metaphor is from the gaming table: Clarke refers it to the arts of gamesters who use false dice that always throw up one number, and Wesley renders it cogging the dice. Clarke is candid about the other figure, saying the tossing refers to some ancient play but what he cannot determine, and guessing at a top or a paper kite.

Whether the next verse means speaking the truth or being true divides them. Barnes takes it as speaking, and requires the simple unvarnished truth against all trick and art and cunning and fraud. Ellicott renders it being true in love, which includes being true to others but also being true absolutely, loving the truth and clinging to it at all costs — and argues that this second element is what properly stands opposed to the childish instability just described. Calvin's editor agrees that the participle denotes not so much speaking the truth as embracing it, and quotes Pythagoras for the two loveliest gifts of the gods to men, to embrace the truth and to be beneficent.

Clarke turns the clause into a rule for controversy, and it is the sharpest thing in the entry. The truth here is the whole system of Gospel doctrine, and since it is the doctrine of God's eternal love to mankind it must be preached in love; scolding and abuse from the pulpit or press are truly monstrous, and he who has the truth of God needs no means to defend it but those that love to God and man provides. Robertson says the same in six words: if truth were always spoken only in love.

On the body Ellicott corrects the English again: that which every joint supplieth is paraphrastic and inaccurate, and should be every contact with the supply from the head, the noun being almost technical for the outflow of strength and nervous energy. Clarke, borrowing Macknight, presses the anatomy — as the human body is formed by the union of all the members under the head and by each member's fitness for its own office, so the church is formed by the union of its members under Christ — and remarks that not the ideas only but the whole phraseology is anatomical. Robertson observes that modern knowledge of cell life greatly strengthens the force of the figure. Gill reads the clause devotionally, taking the body's being from Christ to name its origin, dependence and union, so close as to be indissoluble.
17:
Henry marks the turn: the exhortation to love and concord being finished, what follows is an exhortation to purity and holiness, general first and then in particular instances, urged on their consciences by the apostle's authority from Christ. Ellicott traces a three-stage escalation in the way it is introduced. This I say is what Paul uses when returning from lofty reasoning that not all can follow to solid ground that all may tread; not content with it here, he adds the adjuration I testify, which means he calls God to witness; and not content with that, he adds in the Lord, so the whole form is of peculiar solemnity. Chrysostom explains why such weight is needed and then notices what Paul avoids. It is the teacher's duty to build up his disciples not only by counselling but by alarming them, since when words from fellow-servants will not kindle the soul the case must be made over to God. Yet Paul does not say walk no longer as ye are now walking, which would have struck too hard; he indicates the same thing while taking his example from others.

Whether the darkened understanding is a judgment or a consequence is where they part. Barnes denies the judicial reading outright: the apostle does not say the darkening was judicial, or that they could not have perceived the truth, but states a fact seen now as well as then, that the understanding is darkened by indulgence in sin — the intemperate has no just view of the appetites, the unchaste no perception of purity, so that vice destroys the intellect as well as the body. Gill traces it to the fall: man's understanding was at first filled with natural and divine knowledge, but being ambitious of being as God, he lost what he had. Clarke makes it cumulative, a heart naturally dark growing darker by habitual transgression, and adds that this foolishness made the Gentiles addicted to idolatry, fondly imagining help could come from gods that were the work of their own hands.

The phrase the life of God is unique, as Ellicott notes, and he construes it on the analogy of the righteousness of God, as the life God gives. Calvin offers two senses — what is accounted life in God's sight, or the life he bestows on his elect by regeneration — and says the meaning comes to the same; then he distinguishes three lives in this world: the animal life of motion and bodily sense which we share with the brutes, the human life we have as children of Adam, and the supernatural life which believers alone obtain. On the hardening Robertson supplies the medical sense, a term of Hippocrates for callous hardening.

At the last verse a textual variant is reported by two. Gill notes that the Latin, Syriac and Arabic versions and an old Greek copy read not past feeling but despairing of mercy and salvation, and so growing hardened in sin; Clarke reports the same variant and glosses it of men who from their manner of life could not hope for blessedness hereafter, and might find it in their interest to deny the resurrection and the immortality of the soul. On the received reading Wesley gives the best account of why the word matters: it means past feeling pain, and pain is what urges the sick to seek a remedy, little thought of where there is none.

That they gave themselves over raises the obvious question against the parallel epistle, and Barnes answers it: there God is said to have given them up, and there is no inconsistency, since whatever God's agency in it, they themselves preferred it. Calvin describes the process: those destitute of the Spirit give loose reins to self-indulgence until fresh offences bring down God's wrath, the accusing conscience still speaking but serving only to harden them.
20:
Two report the same alternative pointing of the opening clause. Gill notes that some divide the words into two propositions — but ye are not so; ye have learned Christ — the first looking back to the Gentiles just described; Clarke gives the same repointing. Whether the Christ here is distinguished from Jesus in the next verse then divides the two grammarians sharply. Ellicott holds the name is used emphatically in distinction from Jesus, so that to learn the Christ is to enter into the meaning of his office as anointed Priest, Prophet and King, in one word as Mediator. Robertson takes the opposite view: it is not clear what Paul's precise idea is, but the Cerinthian Gnostics distinguished the man Jesus from the aeon Christ, and Paul here identifies the two.

How much doubt the conditional carries is also disputed. Ellicott says the word indicates no real doubt but strong affirmation, and Robertson calls it a condition of the first class, assumed true. Barnes alone lets a genuine hesitation stand, allowing that a slight and delicate doubt may be implied whether they had attentively listened, though he records Doddridge's rendering, seeing ye have heard him. Ellicott then corrects the rendering of the second verb: they were taught not by him, as the English has it, but in him, in that unity with him which embraces teachers and taught alike as with an atmosphere of his presence.

Calvin makes the passage a test of professed knowledge. He whose life does not differ from an unbeliever's has learned nothing of Christ, since the knowledge of Christ cannot be separated from the mortification of the flesh; and the emphasis on their having been taught reproves that superficial knowledge of the gospel by which many are elated who are wholly unacquainted with newness of life. Hence his distinction between a twofold knowledge of Christ, one genuine and another counterfeit, most men falsely imagining they know him while knowing nothing to the purpose. Wesley states the conclusion in a line: they cannot act thus now they know him, since the Christian dispensation allows of no sin.

What putting off the old man does and does not mean is where Gill is most careful, and his account is the most exact in the chapter. It is not a removing of the old man from the saints, nor a destroying of him, nor a change of his nature; he remains, and remains alive, and is the same old man he ever was in regenerate persons. It is a putting him off from his seat and down from his government — showing no regard to his rule, making no provision for his support, not squaring the life by his directions. Ellicott guards the same clause from the other side, insisting that what is put off is the corruption of the true humanity and not the true humanity itself; and he observes that the word rendered corrupt expresses not so much pollution as disintegration and decay, which carries out the idea implied in calling the man old.

Barnes adds two things nobody else does. He infers from the way these duties are stated that there had probably been teaching of a contrary character at Ephesus, and teachers who did not enforce practical religion. And he limits the renunciation: they are not to lay aside everything that formerly pertained to them, dress and manners and speech not being in question, but only what belonged to a corrupt and fallen nature. Clarke has no such qualification, holding the whole of their former life corrupt and abominable, spent seeking pleasure in the lusts of the flesh and ever deceived by them. Cyril, preaching to candidates, turns the whole passage into an appeal — if any here is a slave of sin, let him promptly prepare himself through faith for the new birth into freedom and adoption.
25:
Chrysostom asks first what falsehood is meant. Idols? Surely not — what is in view is what passes between one man and another. Gill defines the thing carefully and draws the consequences: a lie is a voluntary disagreement of mind and speech with a design to deceive, so that a man may speak what is false and not be a liar if he does not know it to be false, and so that parables and hyperboles are not lies. He then refuses the usual exception, that the officious lie told for another's service is nonetheless unlawful.

Why the command should be needed at all is answered by two, and they differ in the quality of their evidence. Barnes says it may seem strange that Christians should need such an exhortation, and explains it by asserting that lying is the universal vice of the heathen world, ancient and modern alike, citing a jurist long resident in India who would not believe a Hindoo on oath. Clarke makes a narrower version of the same claim and produces sources for it: truth was of small account among even the best heathens, who taught that on many occasions a lie was to be preferred, and he quotes three of them, among them that a lie is better than a hurtful truth.

On the reason Paul actually gives, Ellicott is precise about what he is not saying. Truth is the first condition of the mutual confidence which is the basis of all unity, and so the first duty of that membership one of another which follows from being one body; it is doubtless also a duty to the God who hates a lie, but that view would not be relevant to the apostle's subject here. Wesley puts the same in a line, that all deceit is repugnant to so intimate a union. Calvin steps back to the method: from the righteousness of the new man all godly exhortations flow like streams from a fountain, and all the precepts relating to life, if collected without that principle, would be of little value.

Whether the next clause commands anger, permits it, or warns against it divides them further than anywhere else in the chapter. Robertson calls it a permissive imperative and not a command to be angry. Barnes finds two things implied, that there may be anger without sin and that wherever there is anger there is special danger of sin with it. Gill lists the conditions under which anger is innocent — when it rises from true zeal for God, when it is kindled not against persons but against sins, and when it aims at the good of those we are angry with. Ellicott defends it further still, since our Lord himself felt it at the hardness of men's hearts and it is attributed again and again to God; yet it remains a dangerous and exceptional weapon. Clarke stands against all of them. The Greek here amounts to if ye be angry, do not sin; the sense is rather, take heed that ye be not angry lest ye sin, for it would be very difficult, even for an apostle himself, to be angry and not sin.

The command about the sun draws a classical parallel from two. Barnes reports that the direction conforms to the usage of the Pythagoreans, who when differences arose among them were bound to furnish some token of reconciliation before sunset, and Ellicott notes the same parallel. Robertson locates the danger in a settled mood of anger rather than the first heat. Henry supplies the practical rule for the verse that follows, that we give place to the devil when the first motions of sin are not grievous to our souls, when we consent to them, and when we repeat an evil deed — and that sin is to be resisted by keeping from all appearance of evil.
28:
Gill's definition of theft is the widest here: a fraudulent taking of another's goods without the owner's knowledge, to which he reduces unjust contracts, detention of wages, unlawful usury, and the encouraging and receiving of thieves. Calvin extends it the same way, to concealed depredations no human law punishes, and raises the objection — does Paul oblige all men to labour with their hands? That would be excessively hard. His answer is that the clause is aimed at a particular excuse, since many are in the habit of pleading want; and he adds a rule for choosing a trade, that those employments are to be preferred which yield the greatest advantage to neighbours.

On why converts needed the caution at all, Barnes and Clarke differ in their evidence. Barnes says pilfering prevails in probably every pagan community and argues from habit, that a man long in one sin is in danger of falling into it again; and he draws from the positive clause that no man able to support himself has a right to depend on others. Clarke reports instead that among the rabbins stealing was not entirely discountenanced provided a portion was given to the poor, and answers flatly that if Christianity does not make men honest it does nothing for them. Ellicott sees structure rather than occasion: Paul is not content to forbid dishonesty, nor even to forbid it as fatal to society, but supersedes it by its opposite, so that the thief becomes a giver — striking at the root of the selfishness dishonesty grows from. Robertson notes the tense, cease stealing, and adds that even unemployment is no excuse. Wesley states the principle: whoever has sinned in any kind ought the more zealously to practise the opposite virtue.

The word rendered corrupt is worked over by four. Barnes and Robertson agree it means rotten or putrid, and Barnes extends it to whatever tends to corrupt others. Clarke, following a lexicographer he names, distinguishes three senses — useless, impure, calumnious — and points to the parallel about speech seasoned with salt. Ellicott alone calls the English of the next clause a mistranslation by inversion: it is not the use of edifying but the building up of the need, the supplying of whatever the hearer's state lacks. Calvin weighs the same genitive and prefers to read it of the progress of edification. Wesley makes corrupt discourse all that is not profitable.

At the last verse the question is what grieving can mean of God. Gill says it is spoken by an anthropopathy, and is careful whose spirit is meant — not the believer's own, nor a good man's, but the third person. Barnes agrees the Spirit does not literally endure pain, and takes the expression to describe conduct fitted to cause grief in a friend who loves us; he also notes that the address is to Christians, which proves Christians can do it. Ellicott presses the other way: grieving implies a personal relation more strongly than quenching or resisting do, and he ties the verse to the whole series, since the body is one only because the Spirit is one. Clarke traces the sequel — the Spirit withdraws light and presence, hardness and darkness follow, and worst of all insensibility, the darkness preventing the fallen state from being seen and the hardness from being felt. Calvin records and rejects the reading that we grieve the Spirit in others by offending godly brethren, on the ground that what follows will not bear it. Henry ties both verses to one root, that filthy words proceed from corruption in the speaker and corrupt those who hear, while the Spirit so grieved is the earnest of the redemption day. Cyril, dwelling on the Spirit's work rather than the warning, recalls the wisdom given to Daniel, by which a young man convicted the elders and a condemned woman was saved.
31:
Whether the list ascends or descends is the sharpest disagreement here, and the two who notice its order take opposite views. Ellicott reads a progression in three stages: bitterness first, an acerbity of temper ready to take offence; then wrath and anger, the passionate outburst and the deeper anger of which it is at once effect and cause; then clamour and evil speaking, the loud fury of the first burst passing into the more deliberate slander. Wesley reads the same series backwards, calling it a beautiful retrogradation that begins with the highest degree of the want of love and descends to the lowest — bitterness the height of settled anger, anger the first risings of disgust — and pairs each term with the virtue set against it in the following verse.

What bitterness names is answered four ways. Gill offers a range of senses — the corruption of nature, heretical doctrines, sharp words between saints — and settles on the narrowest, the first offence taken in the mind, to be put away at once. Clarke identifies it with religious censoriousness, those who measure all persons by a fixed standard and unchristian everyone who falls short, and gives it a name from an old compound medicine of acrid drugs called the holy bitter, which he says did immense evil and scarcely ever any good. Chrysostom works by images. Bees will not settle in an unclean vessel, which is why keepers sprinkle the hive with perfumes; the soul is such a vessel, able to receive swarms of spiritual gifts, but if gall and bitterness are in it the swarms fly away. And bile, held within its membrane, does no great mischief; once the vessel bursts, a trifling quantity taints the whole system.

On the individual terms the grammarians divide the synonyms differently. Clarke makes the first word the commencement of the passion and the second the same passion carried to its highest pitch. Calvin says the received distinction is that one denotes the power and the other the act, but holds that here the first is only a more sudden attack; and he observes that removing malice would greatly aid the correction of all the rest. Barnes glosses the list plainly — cherished unreasonable anger, the high words men use in a brawl, slander and backbiting — and corrects the final phrase, which is not malice but every kind of evil. Robertson notes the verb means to pick up and carry away, a clean sweep.

The virtues set opposite are read as manners by some and as temper by others. Barnes makes the first of them courteousness, holds that Christianity produces true politeness and that a Christian should be the most polite of men, and denies that there is any religion in a sour or misanthropic temper, while excepting a hollow-hearted politeness not to be copied. Clarke is briefer and blunter: a Christian cannot be a savage, and he need not be a boor. Ellicott keeps to disposition, kindness being gentleness in bearing with wrong and tenderheartedness a positive warmth of sympathy. Calvin sets the same virtue against the cruelty of iron-hearted men who watch the sufferings of others without concern, and reports a rendering of the participle as beneficence, preferring forgiveness.

On the ground of forgiveness Chrysostom makes the observation the others do not: Paul argues from what has already been done for us rather than from the promise that those who forgive shall be forgiven, since past things have greater force — and the comparison fails anyway, for we forgive a fellow-servant while God forgave a servant, an enemy, and one who hated him. Barnes turns the same clause into a rule: freely, fully, liberally, never raking up old offences, and there is no danger of carrying it too far. Ellicott adds the one limit anyone states, that such forgiveness implies neither condonation of evil nor the withholding of chastisement.
